result:
The flow starts in [src/app/(dashboard)/[orgSlug]/settings/members/page.tsx](src/app/(dashboard)/[orgSlug]/settings/members/page.tsx). It loads the tenant and actor, checks whether the actor can read members and invite, then renders `InviteMemberForm` with the current seat check and `inviteMemberAction`. In [src/components/domain/member/invite-member-form.tsx](src/components/domain/member/invite-member-form.tsx), `handleSubmit` validates the organization ID, email, and role with `inviteMemberSchema`; the UI also disables submission when seats are full. These are usability checks as well as validation, but the server repeats the important authorization and quota checks.

When submitted, `inviteMemberAction` in [src/actions/members/invite-member.ts](src/actions/members/invite-member.ts) runs through `withAction`, which validates the input and resolves the actor. It calls `can` for `member:invite` against the pending-member resource, consumes the organization’s invite rate limit, reads the organization summary, and checks the plan’s seat limit. Then it calls `inviteMember` in [src/server/services/invitation-service.ts](src/server/services/invitation-service.ts). That service checks organization scope and invite permission again, consumes a rate limit per invite, loads the organization, and counts active members plus pending invitations before checking the seat limit again.

For each invite, `inviteMembers` generates a random token and passes its SHA-256 hash to `invitationRepo.insertInvitation`. In [src/server/db/schema/members.ts](src/server/db/schema/members.ts), the `invitations` table stores the organization, email, role, inviter, token hash, expiration, and accepted/revoked timestamps. The repository sets a 14-day expiration and leaves `acceptedAt` and `revokedAt` null. There is no pending membership row at this stage.

There is an important mismatch in the current implementation: `randomToken(32)` creates a raw token, but the service passes only `hashToken(token)` to the repository and never returns or sends the raw token. `toInvitation` in [src/server/repositories/_mappers.ts](src/server/repositories/_mappers.ts) maps the stored `tokenHash` into the `Invitation.token` field. The invitation email component in [src/emails/invite-email.tsx](src/emails/invite-email.tsx) exists, but this flow does not call an email sender or construct an invite URL. So, as written, this path does not produce a usable link containing the raw token; passing the mapped `Invitation.token` back would fail because acceptance hashes the supplied token before looking it up. The acceptance path below describes what the code attempts to do if it receives the original raw token.

On invitation creation, the service emits `member.invited` with the organization, inviter, email, and role. The activity listener in [src/server/services/activity-service.ts](src/server/services/activity-service.ts) records an “invited” activity entry. The action revalidates member and invitation views. No email delivery is triggered by the shown invitation service.

When someone opens `/invite/[token]`, `Page` in [src/app/(auth)/invite/[token]/page.tsx](src/app/(auth)/invite/[token]/page.tsx) validates the token’s shape. If there is no session, it redirects to login with the invite URL as `next`; after sign-in, the page shows the signed-in principal’s email and an accept button. The page does not look up the token or check that the signed-in email matches the invitation email. The form in [src/app/(auth)/invite/[token]/invite-accept-form.tsx](src/app/(auth)/invite/[token]/invite-accept-form.tsx) submits the token to `acceptInvitationAction` in [src/actions/members/accept-invitation.ts](src/actions/members/accept-invitation.ts).

That action validates the token, requires a signed-in principal via `getSessionPrincipal`, and calls `acceptInvitation`. In the service, the token is hashed and looked up by `findInvitationByTokenHash` in [src/server/repositories/invitation-repository.ts](src/server/repositories/invitation-repository.ts). The service rejects a missing, revoked, already accepted, or expired invitation. It then checks whether the signed-in user already has a membership in the organization; if so, it returns that existing member. Otherwise it inserts an active membership with the invitation’s role and inviter, marks the invitation accepted, and emits `member.joined`.

After that insert, `acceptInvitationAction` calls `assertSeatAvailable`: it resolves an actor from the new membership and checks organization usage against the plan limit. This check happens after the membership and accepted timestamp have been written, so a seat-limit error can be reported after those changes have already occurred.

Once the membership exists, `resolveActor` in [src/server/services/member-service.ts](src/server/services/member-service.ts), and `resolveActorForOrg` in [src/server/services/session-service.ts](src/server/services/session-service.ts), can derive an `Actor` from the active membership’s user, organization, and role. That actor is what the rest of the server uses for organization scoping and permission checks. The membership repository’s active-member counts and member lists now include the person; organization listing can include the workspace for that user; and the `member.joined` listeners update seat usage in [src/server/services/usage-service.ts](src/server/services/usage-service.ts) and notify the organization owner in [src/server/services/notification-service.ts](src/server/services/notification-service.ts). The membership row itself is stored in the `members` table, with `status: "active"`, the assigned role, inviter, and join timestamp.
